# The seven-minute talk {#sec-talk}

The script for the lightning talk, with timings. The deck it goes with is
`slides/lightning-talk.qmd`.

Seven minutes is roughly 1,000 spoken words. That is enough for **one** idea
with **three** supporting beats. The idea here is:

> Graph embeddings turn structure into vectors, the main algorithms are all the
> same algorithm wearing different hats, and the payoff is that a transformer
> can finally see your graph.

Everything that does not serve that gets cut. In particular the talk does not
cover: GraphSAGE sampling, over-smoothing, evaluation methodology, or node2vec's
$p$ and $q$. Those are what the book is for, and the last slide says so.

---

Slides 4 and 5 are the ones to cut into if you are running long: drop the code

## The script

### Slide 1 — Title (0:00)

> Graph embeddings, in R. Seven minutes, four algorithms, and one demo where
> the accuracy goes from 11% to 96%.

### Slide 2 — The problem (0:15)

> Here is a graph. Thirty-four people in a karate club in the 1970s, and who was
> friends with whom. The club had a falling-out and split in two, and the
> question people have been asking of this dataset for fifty years is: could you
> have predicted the split from the friendships?
>
> Now, to do anything statistical with this you need a table. One row per
> person, a fixed number of columns. What you have is an adjacency matrix, and
> it is the wrong shape in three ways. It is 34 columns wide, so it changes
> shape when someone joins. It is 87% zeros. And worst of all, it has no
> geometry — two people three hops apart in the same tight friendship group look
> exactly as unrelated as two people in different countries.
>
> An adjacency matrix records edges. What you want is similarity. And in a
> graph, similarity comes from paths, not from single entries.

### Slide 3 — The idea (1:00)

> So: a graph embedding is a map from each node to a short dense vector — say 32
> numbers — chosen so that *close in the vector space* means *structurally
> close in the graph*.
>
> Here is the karate club embedded into two dimensions. Colour is the faction
> people actually joined. The algorithm never saw those labels, and the first
> axis alone gets 33 of the 34 people right.
>
> Look at the one in the middle. That is node 9, who joined the officers'
> faction despite being better connected to the instructor's side. A method
> that was overconfident would have put him firmly on one side. This one puts
> him in the middle, which is the honest answer.

### Slide 4 — Spectral (1:50)

> Four algorithms. The first is the oldest and it is four lines of R.
>
> Write down what you want: connected nodes should be close. So penalise every
> edge by the squared gap it has to stretch. Expand that square and it collapses
> into a quadratic form in the matrix $D - A$ — degree matrix minus adjacency.
> That is the graph Laplacian, and the whole field runs on this identity.
>
> Minimise it, constrain it so it can't collapse to zero, and the answer is
> eigenvectors. Take the ones with the smallest eigenvalues — the smoothest
> non-constant functions on the graph. That is the picture you just saw.
>
> Bonus: the eigenvalues tell you how many communities there are. Three near
> zero, then a jump, means three communities. You get that for free.

### Slide 5 — Random walks (2:50)

> Second algorithm. 2014, and someone notices that word2vec is doing something
> suspiciously relevant.
>
> Word2vec learns word vectors from "words that appear near each other are
> related". DeepWalk's move is: a random walk on a graph *is* a sentence. Start
> anywhere, step to a random neighbour, forty times. Do that ten times per node.
> Now you have a corpus, and the nodes are the words.
>
> Then run skip-gram: every node gets a vector, real co-occurring pairs should
> score high, random pairs should score low. Logistic regression against noise.
> The gradient is one line, and I've written it out in the book — it's about
> sixty lines of R with no autodiff.
>
> On the karate club this recovers the factions perfectly. And crucially,
> nothing here is quadratic in the number of nodes, which is why this is the
> family that scaled to billions of edges.

### Slide 6 — They're all the same algorithm (3:50)

> Now the part I actually want you to remember.
>
> In 2018 Qiu and co-authors proved that DeepWalk is not really a neural
> method. Skip-gram with negative sampling provably converges to a factorisation
> of a pointwise-mutual-information matrix — that's Levy and Goldberg, 2014 —
> and for random walks on a graph, that matrix has a closed form. It's this: the
> transition matrix $P$, summed over powers 1 to T, times $D$ inverse, log of
> the whole thing.
>
> So you can skip the walks and the gradient descent entirely and just take an
> SVD. In the book I check this: the learned dot products correlate 0.98 with
> the PMI the theory predicts, and the sampled matrix converges to the exact one
> as you draw more walks.
>
> Same accuracy on the karate club. About a thousand times faster.
>
> Every method on this slide is a low-rank factorisation of some matrix built
> from $A$. They differ in *which matrix*. That's it.

### Slide 7 — GNNs (4:30)

> Which also tells you the ceiling. Every one of those is a function of $A$
> alone. It can't use the fact that a node is a 34-year-old who joined in March,
> and it can't embed anyone who wasn't there when you factorised.
>
> Graph neural networks fix both by replacing the lookup table with a function:
> average your neighbours' features, multiply by a shared weight matrix, repeat.
> Shared weights, so new nodes just get a forward pass.
>
> Two things worth knowing. A GCN layer is a learned smoother — so if you stack
> twenty of them every node converges to the same vector, which is why GNNs are
> almost always two or three layers deep. And graph attention, GAT, is
> self-attention with the adjacency matrix as its mask.
>
> Which raises the question: what if you took the mask off?

### Slide 8 — Into a transformer (5:00)

> Self-attention has no idea what order its inputs are in. Permute them and the
> output permutes with them. That's why transformers need positional encodings
> — and text has an obvious order to encode. A graph doesn't.
>
> So: how do you tell a permutation-invariant architecture about a structure
> with no canonical ordering? Three doors.
>
> One: use graph embeddings as your input vectors. If your tokens are entities
> that also live in a graph — clinical codes in a vocabulary hierarchy, products
> in a catalogue — embed the graph offline and initialise the embedding table.
> Zero architecture changes, and the rare tokens benefit most.
>
> Two: structural positional encodings. Feed each node its Laplacian
> eigenvectors — literally the spectral embedding from slide 4. That analogy is
> exact, by the way: sine waves are the eigenvectors of the Laplacian of a
> line graph.
>
> Three, and this is the interesting one: put the graph inside the attention
> computation.

### Slide 9 — The result (5:45)

> Graphormer's trick. Attention scores are query dot key over root d. Add one
> more term: a learnable scalar indexed by the shortest-path distance between
> the two nodes. That's it.
>
> Here's what it does. Ninety nodes, three communities. I reveal the true
> community for 40% of them and zero out the rest, and the model has to infer
> the others. The content-based part of attention is deliberately uninformative,
> so the only route to the answer is the graph.
>
> Without the bias, attention is flat — 33% of its mass lands on your own
> community, which is exactly chance, because a third of the graph *is* your
> community. The transformer is blind. Add the distance bias and that goes to
> 88%. You can see it in the attention matrix: the block structure appears.
>
> Downstream test accuracy: 11% without, 96% with. Same architecture, same
> features, same parameter count. One scalar per distance, added before the
> softmax.

### Slide 10 — Takeaways (6:35)

> Three things.
>
> Graph embeddings turn structure into geometry, and they're small — I wrote all
> four from scratch in base R.
>
> They're all the same algorithm: a low-rank factorisation of a matrix built
> from the adjacency. Before you reach for a library, try an SVD, and always run
> "count the mutual friends" as a baseline — it wins more often than anyone
> admits.
>
> And if you're putting a transformer near a graph, the structure has to get in
> somewhere. Input vectors, positional encodings, or attention bias. Pick at
> least one.
>
> Book and code are at the link. Thank you.

---

## Delivery notes

**Rehearse slide 6.** It is the intellectual core and the easiest to garble.
Practise saying "pointwise mutual information" until it is one word.

**Do not read the code on slides 4 and 5.** It is there so the audience can see
how short it is. Say "four lines" and move on.

**The pause is on slide 9.** After "11% without, 96% with", stop for a beat
before the last sentence. It is the only number anyone will remember.

**If you are asked "does this beat a GNN?"** --- the honest answer is: on a
fixed featureless graph, usually not by much, and NetMF is a much harder
baseline than people expect. The GNN earns its keep when you have node features
or a changing graph.

**If you are asked about scale** --- NetMF as written is $O(n^3)$ and dense.
Past about 20,000 nodes, use sparse spectral methods or go back to sampled
walks. The sampling that looks unnecessary is exactly what makes it scale.

**If you overrun**, cut slide 7 to one sentence: "GNNs add node features and
handle new nodes; a GAT is masked self-attention." It buys you thirty seconds
and slide 8 follows from it anyway.
